origin: Original workshop built by Muse (AI assistant) on 19 November 2026 at Steven Powell's direction, from his own notes in the Everyday Cool ideas side chat that evening. Of the four queued STEM rooms he ordered saved that night (Math, Engineering, Earth, Computing — 'save that list I want to do them all'), Engineering went first and Math second; Earth is third, on his tap of the option card: 'Everyday Earth next.' His notes, built to here: his one-line sketch in the saved queue — 'looking down instead of up: weather, rocks, soil, the water cycle'; his follow-up order to include 'links to weather, and tonight's sky in it as well'; his standing order that the STEM rooms carry Wikipedia and other links on their pages (fifteen destinations, verified live); a late addition sent mid-build — Earth Day info (earthday.org) and a UC Davis link on the earth-relevant side, his alma mater — which the room carries with the two origin threads kept straight: UC Davis ran one of the first Earth Day celebrations anywhere (Whole Earth Week, 17–21 March 1970, from John McConnell's concept via an Experimental College student and José Argüelles's ~400 students, per the UC Davis Library's own traditions exhibit), a month before Gaylord Nelson's April 22 founding, which the shelf does not claim for Davis; and the banner to his concept, in his words: 'AI looking at maps and a globe' — the plush robot studying a globe with a topographic map and a weather map spread on the desk. The room: the water cycle as a four-stage tappable loop with the USGS's ~90% ocean-evaporation share and the 'older than the dinosaurs' claim carrying its honest edges; the rock sorter, nine rocks in three families told by birth; soil in its five horizons with the centuries-an-inch topsoil range; the depth bench over a true-scale bar (crust given its deepest figure, 70 km, and still a hairline; deepest mine 3.9 km, trench 10.9 km, borehole 12.3 km, all still crust); and weather from the ground — cold and warm fronts, four cloud families, and a barometer bench whose printed limit is that a forecast is a probability, not a promise. It enters the catalog under 'Science' with hubParent 'stem-room', immediately after Everyday Math, as the twenty-eighth entry and the STEM Room's ninth workshop. This folder is the maintained original. Web-first, per Steven's plan set the same evening: the four queue rooms go live on the web one at a time and reach the desktop app together in a single later release.
